meta.titre: Linear and Quadratic Inequalities: Signs, Intervals and Critical Values
meta.sous_theme: Solving linear, compound and quadratic inequalities

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Additional Mathematics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A trader in Bamenda must sell enough bags of groundnuts to cover her daily costs, and the answer to her question is not one number but a whole range of numbers. Mathematicians write such a range with an inequality, and the same idea decides how many items a business must sell to make a profit or which dimensions keep an area below a limit. In the GCE papers, linear inequalities give quick marks in Paper 1, while quadratic inequalities in Paper 2 reward students who know how to read the graph of a quadratic. Careful sign handling is what separates full marks from a lost mark.

items: The symbols $<$ and $>$ exclude the end value, while $\le$ and $\ge$ include it.
On a number line an open circle excludes the end value and a filled circle includes it.
A quadratic expression can be factorised, and $(x-p)(x-q)=0$ gives $x=p$ or $x=q$.
Multiplying a positive number by a negative number gives a negative number.

sections.titre: Solving inequalities and reading the sign of a quadratic
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Linear inequalities Solve them like equations, with one exception: **when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, the inequality sign is reversed.** For example, $-2x<6$ gives $x>-3$, because dividing by $-2$ turns $<$ into $>$. Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides never changes the sign. ### Compound inequalities An inequality such as $a<\text{expression}\le b$ is solved by doing the same operation on all three parts. The answer is written in the same form, for example $-20 \iff x

variantes.nom: Compound inequality with a negative coefficient
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the unknown term has a negative coefficient, as in $2\le7-x<5$.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Subtract $7$ from every part: $-5\le-x<-2$. Multiply every part by $-1$ and reverse both signs: $5\ge x>2$. Written in increasing order, **$2<x\le5$**. Check: $x=5$ gives $7-5=2$, which satisfies $2\le 2$; $x=2$ gives $5$, which is not less than $5$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the critical values are not whole numbers, so the quadratic formula is needed.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
To solve $x^{2}-4x-1<0$, solve $x^{2}-4x-1=0$ with $x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$: $x=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{20}}{2}=2\pm\sqrt5$.

Since the inequality is "less than zero", the solution lies between the critical values: **$2-\sqrt5<x<2+\sqrt5$**. Keep the exact surds in the answer unless the question asks for decimals.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the expression starts with $-x^{2}$, which would flip the picture of the graph.
variantes.contenu_markdown: To solve $-x^{2}+2x+3\ge0$, multiply by $-1$ and reverse the sign: $x^{2}-2x-3\le0$. Then $(x-3)(x+1)\le0$ and **$-1\le x\le3$**. Check with $x=0$: $3\ge0$ is true, and $0$ lies in the interval.

sections.enonce_markdown: A rectangular vegetable plot has width $x$ metres and length $(x+6)$ metres. The farmer wants its area to be less than $40$ square metres. Find the possible values of $x$.

etapes.action: Translate the condition into an inequality.
etapes.justification: Area equals length times width, and the area must be less than $40$.

etapes.action: Rearrange so that one side is zero.
etapes.justification: A quadratic inequality is solved by comparing with zero. Expand the bracket first.

etapes.action: Factorise to find the critical values.
etapes.justification: Two numbers with product $-40$ and sum $6$ are $10$ and $-4$.

etapes.action: Apply the rule for "less than zero".
etapes.justification: The graph of the U-shaped curve is below the axis between its two roots.

etapes.action: Apply the condition of the problem.
etapes.justification: A width cannot be negative or zero, so only the positive part of the interval is possible.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The width must satisfy $0<x<4$: it is a positive number less than $4$ metres.

items.pourquoi_faux: Dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality. Test $x=-5$: $-3(-5)=15>12$ is true, but $-5$ is not greater than $-4$.
The numbers $-5$ or $-10$ give $x<4$ but have squares larger than $16$. Both $4$ and $-4$ are critical values.
A product is positive when both brackets are positive and also when both are negative. The second case is lost. Test $x=-4$: $(-6)(-1)=6>0$.

items.erreur_markdown: $x^{2}>3x$: divide both sides by $x$ to get $x>3$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The sign of $x$ is not known, so dividing by $x$ may reverse the inequality, and the case $x<0$ is lost. Test $x=-1$: $1>-3$ is true.

items.erreur_markdown: The solution is $x<1$ or $x>3$, which I write as $3<x<1$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The chain $3<x<1$ asks for numbers that are greater than $3$ and less than $1$ at the same time, and no such number exists.

items.solution_markdown:
(a) Expand: $3x+6>4x-1$. Subtract $3x$ from both sides: $6>x-1$. Add $1$: $7>x$. The solution is **$x<7$**.

(b) Subtract $7$: $-2x\ge-6$. Divide by $-2$ and reverse the sign: $x\le3$. The solution is **$x\le3$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Find the range of values of $x$ for which $-7\le5-2x<3$.

(b) Solve the inequality $x^{2}-3x-10<0$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Subtract $5$ from every part: $-12\le-2x<-2$. Divide every part by $-2$ and reverse both signs: $6\ge x>1$. In increasing order: **$1<x\le6$**.

(b) Factorise: $(x-5)(x+2)<0$. The critical values are $-2$ and $5$, and "less than zero" means between them: **$-2<x<5$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Find the values of $x$ that satisfy both $x^{2}-2x-8\ge0$ and $2x+1<7$.

(b) List all the integers $x$ that satisfy $x^{2}-2x-5<0$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) First inequality: $(x-4)(x+2)\ge0$, so $x\le-2$ or $x\ge4$. Second inequality: $2x<6$, so $x<3$.

Both must hold. The part $x\ge4$ does not satisfy $x<3$, while $x\le-2$ does. The solution is **$x\le-2$**.

(b) Solve $x^{2}-2x-5=0$: $x=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4+20}}{2}=1\pm\sqrt6$, which is about $-1.449$ and $3.449$. The inequality "less than zero" holds between them: $1-\sqrt6<x<1+\sqrt6$.

The integers in this interval are **$-1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3$**. (Check $x=3$: $9-6-5=-2<0$; check $x=4$: $16-8-5=3$, not less than $0$.)

items_markdown: Solve a linear inequality like an equation, but reverse the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number.
For a compound inequality, do the same operation on all three parts, and write the answer in increasing order.
For a quadratic inequality, make one side zero, find the critical values, then decide: between them for $<0$, outside them (with "or") for $>0$.
Never divide by an expression that contains $x$; factorise instead.
Finish by checking the conditions of the problem (positive length, whole numbers) and test one value from your answer.
